title: Prevent chronic hepatitis C infection with a licensed vaccine

concept.text: Prevent establishment of chronic HCV infection after exposure, including in people at continuing risk of reinfection. A 548-participant randomized vaccine trial induced immune responses but failed to prevent chronic infection. Proposed completion test: Regulatory licensure following a randomized field efficacy trial showing significantly fewer incident chronic HCV infections than control, using a prespecified persistent-infection endpoint and at least 12 months of exposure follow-up. Test set by: A regulator would decide licensure. The NIAID-funded trial defined chronic infection as persistent viraemia for six months; the follow-up minimum here is editorial. Overlaps: VIR-04. Sources given: [Randomized HCV vaccine trial](https://www.nejm.org/doi/pdf/10.1056/NEJMoa2023345?articleTools=true) ; [WHO hepatitis C factsheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hepatitis-c).

page.title: Licensed prophylactic hepatitis C vaccine
page.definition: A licensed preventive vaccine reduces the risk that exposure to hepatitis C virus (HCV) leads to chronic infection: persistence of viral RNA in blood for six months.

goal.need: WHO reports that about 70% (55–85%) of people infected with HCV develop chronic infection. Among people with chronic infection, 15–30% develop cirrhosis within 20 years. Its fact sheet dated 28 July 2026 reports no effective HCV vaccine.

completion.title: FDA licenses a vaccine with an indication covering prevention of chronic hepatitis C infection.
completion.criterion: FDA issues a biologics licence for a preventive HCV vaccine, with an approved indication covering prevention of chronic HCV infection in a specified population. FDA determines that the clinical evidence establishes safety and effectiveness, that benefits outweigh risks for that population, and that manufacturing and facility information establish product quality and consistency.
completion.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 601.4 and Vaccine Development – 101; these are general vaccine licensure requirements.
completion.threshold_quote: the establishment(s) and the product meet the applicable requirements established in this chapter.
completion.basis: Licensure supplies an external decision covering clinical benefit, safety and manufacturing. FDA bases the approved indication on satisfactory supporting data. WHO reports that no effective HCV vaccine exists. No HCV-specific minimum efficacy percentage or protection duration was identified in the regulatory sources searched.

milestones.title: An HCV vaccine passes preclinical review and enters an authorised human study.
milestones.criterion: Laboratory and animal studies characterize vaccine-induced immunity and toxicity sufficiently for FDA to permit human testing under an Investigational New Drug application. WHO specifies nonclinical immunogenicity and safety assessment. This regulatory stage was reached by ChAd3-NSmut/MVA-NSmut: its 548-participant human study, conducted during 2012–2018, operated under an FDA-reviewed IND protocol.
milestones.set_by: FDA, preclinical and IND assessment in Vaccine Development – 101, supported by WHO TRS 927, Annex 1, sections 3–4; these criteria concern vaccines generally.
milestones.threshold_quote: whether it is reasonably safe for testing of the vaccine to move forward in people.

milestones.title: An HCV vaccine elicits human immune responses and clears safety review for phase 2.
milestones.criterion: Human studies demonstrate vaccine-induced immune responses and a safety profile permitting progression to phase 2. A study published on 5 November 2014 enrolled 15 healthy adults; all 9 evaluated recipients of ChAd3-NSmut/MVA-NSmut developed HCV-specific T-cell responses, and no serious adverse reactions were reported. In NCT01436357, the monitoring board recommended phase 2 after 68 participants had enrolled.
milestones.set_by: FDA, phase 1-to-phase 2 progression in Vaccine Development – 101; the reported HCV results concern the ChAd3-NSmut/MVA-NSmut candidate.
milestones.threshold_quote: the absence of safety concerns from phase 1 studies

milestones.title: An HCV vaccine significantly reduces six-month persistent infection in a randomized field trial.
milestones.criterion: Vaccination reduces six-month persistent HCV infection versus placebo in adults who inject drugs, in the prespecified per-protocol analysis with a two-sided log-rank test at α=0.05. Persistence requires sequence-confirmed infection with the same virus initially and at month 6, plus an intervening RNA-positive sample. Follow-up was monthly for 20 months after enrolment and for 9 months after infection detection. The 548-participant study published on 11 February 2021 failed: chronic infection occurred in 14/261 vaccine recipients and 14/259 controls; hazard ratio 1.53 (95% CI 0.66–3.55).
milestones.set_by: Investigators of NIAID-sponsored protocol NCT01436357, as reported in its trial publication; this is the candidate's field-efficacy test.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary efficacy end point was chronic HCV infection, defined as persistent viremia for 6 months.

milestones.title: An HCV vaccine completes phase 3 studies and FDA files its licence application.
milestones.criterion: Phase 3 studies supply effectiveness and safety evidence, and commercial manufacturing development supports consistent production. FDA receives the complete Biologics License Application, including nonclinical and clinical results, manufacturing methods, stability data and proposed labelling, and considers it filed for review. FDA describes successful clinical development and a reproducible manufacturing process as preceding this submission.
milestones.set_by: FDA, vaccine development pathway and filing requirements in 21 CFR 601.2(a); these requirements concern biological products generally.
milestones.threshold_quote: An application for a biologics license shall not be considered as filed until all pertinent information and data have been received

not_found: Searches of WHO preferred-product-characteristic resources and FDA guidance found no HCV-specific minimum vaccine efficacy or required protection duration for licensure.
No published efficacy threshold specifically requiring protection against reinfection after HCV cure was found.
The NEJM-hosted trial article and supplement could not be opened; an author-manuscript copy of the article was available.
ClinicalTrials.gov did not expose the study record's details through the accessible page.
The 1994 chimpanzee vaccination paper could not be opened in a readable primary-source version.

results.finding: In 9 evaluated ChAd3-NSmut/MVA-NSmut recipients, all 9 developed HCV-specific T-cell responses.
results.detail: The phase 1 study enrolled 15 volunteers and reported no serious adverse reactions. It says an efficacy study had started, but does not report a safety review recommending progression to phase 2.
results.quote:
HCV-specific T cell responses were significantly enhanced by MVA-
NSmut boost in all volunteers, peaking 1 week after vaccination (median,
2355; range, 1490 to 6117 SFCs/106 PBMCs; peak after ChAd3-NSmut
prime versus peak after MVA-NSmut boost;P = 0.0039; Fig. 1, A and B).
